keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. The colony 'established by the Kingdom of Great Britain in 1763' by the Royal Proclamation of 7 October 1763 had boundaries that 'did not extend as far west as the Great Lakes or as far north as Rupert's Land'; the page gives no area. The gazetteer's St Lawrence region is about 0.42 M km2. Under military government 1760-1764 (civil government only from 1764).

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. The Quebec Act of 22 June 1774 'enlarged the boundaries of Quebec to include the Ohio Country' and part of the Illinois Country, 'extending west to the Mississippi River and north to the southern boundary of Rupert's Land'; the Quebec Act page: 'roughly tripling its size'. The shape is about 1.73 M km2 (gazetteer), 4.2 times the 1763 shape (0.42 M km2) against the page's 'roughly tripling': the Ohio and Illinois states are drawn whole (the act's western limit was the Mississippi and its southern limit the Ohio, so Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan and Wisconsin overshoot slightly and the 1763 shape may be small); within a factor of two of the page. The Labrador dispute page adds that the Quebec Act gave Quebec 'control over lands that had been assigned to Newfoundland in 1763' (the Labrador coast), which is drawn.

'Established by the Kingdom of Great Britain in 1763' after the conquest of New France; infobox Royal Proclamation 7 October 1763; 'As part of the 1763 Treaty of Paris, France gave up its claim to the colony.' The page names no boundary beyond the two negatives, so the St Lawrence valley is the researcher's reading.

ledger.note: 1774: the Quebec Act enlarges the province. Royal assent on 22 June 1774; 'The act expanded the province to include much of what is now southern Ontario, Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Ohio, Wisconsin, and parts of Minnesota, roughly tripling its size.' New York, Pennsylvania and Virginia were angered because their charters had granted them the Ohio lands. The Province of Quebec page adds 'extending west to the Mississippi River and north to the southern boundary of Rupert's Land'.

certainty.note: The Proclamation named the colony's limits only in the negative (not to the Great Lakes, not to Rupert's Land).
The Quebec Act boundaries ran to the Mississippi and the Ohio but were not surveyed.
The 1783 line through the Great Lakes was not fixed on the ground until the Jay Treaty of 1795 (Upper Canada page).

notes: Not a Cliopatria row (Cliopatria draws these years inside 'New France' to 1791 and 'British Colonial Empire'). Two pages: Province of Quebec (1763-1791) and Quebec Act. Not on the pages: the area, the Proclamation's 45th-parallel and Saint-Jean boundaries, Anticosti and the Magdalen Islands (both in the Quebec dossier's gap), the American invasion of 1775-76, the British forts south of the lakes held until the Jay Treaty. Disagreement: the Quebec Act page infobox has commencement 13 January 1774, before royal assent on 22 June 1774. The New France dossier ends in February 1763 and records the cession to british-colonial-empire; the 'new-france' counterpart here is the colony of Canada, the same land. The 1774 gain of the Ohio and Illinois lands is recorded from 'nobody' (Native land), that of the Labrador coast from dominion-of-newfoundland; the Quebec Act page says New York, Pennsylvania and Virginia held charters over the Ohio lands (the thirteen-colonies dossier does not draw them). Region names the gazetteer already has: all.
